posts.title: Five questions before you open a spreadsheet
posts.excerpt: Write the question first. The spreadsheet can wait ten minutes.
posts.content:
Most analysis goes wrong before any data is opened. Someone asks for “a look at returns” and an afternoon disappears into columns. Before you open the file, answer five questions on paper.

Who will read the result, and what will they decide? What would a useful answer look like in one sentence? What data could possibly answer it, and who owns that data? What would make you change your mind? And when is it due?

Five lines, written by hand. If you cannot answer them, the work is not ready to start, and that is worth knowing early. Module 1 of the course is built around this habit.

Lesson 1.3, “Where good questions come from”, is free to watch and covers the first two questions in 11 minutes.

posts.title: A tidy column is a kind gesture
posts.excerpt: Clean data is a favour to the next person, who is often you.
posts.content:
A column that mixes “12 March”, “3/12” and “last Tuesday” is a small unkindness. Whoever opens the file next, including you in six months, has to guess what you meant.

Tidy data has one thing per column and one row per case. Dates look like dates, names are spelled one way, and an empty cell means something you have decided.

Keep a cleaning log: a short list of what you changed and why. It takes minutes and makes your result checkable by someone else, which is the whole point of analysis.

Module 2 teaches this slowly, with the small disasters that real exports produce.

posts.title: Why the bakery chart is a bar chart
posts.excerpt: Daniel’s weekly baking plan, and the chart choice behind it.
posts.content:
Daniel Kowalski, who owns a neighbourhood bakery, first drew his sales as a smooth line. It looked impressive and told him nothing about Tuesdays.

Seven bars, one per weekday, with rainy days in a darker shade, showed the pattern at a glance. Bars compare categories; lines show change over time. His question was about weekdays, so bars were right.

The chart led to a plain weekly baking plan. There is less leftover bread, which he can see on his own shelf.

Choosing the chart is the whole of Module 5. The rule of thumb: pick the chart that answers the question in ten seconds.

posts.title: What a project review looks like
posts.excerpt: Priya’s written feedback has the same four parts every time.
posts.content:
Every project in the course gets a written review from Priya Raman or Kazu Moreno, returned within 5 working days.

A review has four parts: what the question was, whether the method fits it, whether the chart says what you meant, and one next step. We keep it short on purpose.

Reviews do not grade you. They say what a careful colleague would say, so you can fix it and move on.

If you want to talk it through, a 45-minute video call is available for €70.

posts.title: SQL is just asking in order
posts.excerpt: Four verbs cover most of what an analyst needs.
posts.content:
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY. Say them as a sentence: show me these columns, from this table, where this is true, grouped by that.

Once you read a query as a sentence, joins stop being frightening. A join is just a second table you are asking to stand next to the first.

Amara Osei used exactly this to join three return logs and find the size chart that was causing repeat returns.

Module 3 has nine lessons and one project, and costs €95 on its own.

posts.title: How we record a lesson
posts.excerpt: A desk, a microphone and Tomás checking every caption.
posts.content:
Lessons are recorded in the Rotterdam studio, mostly in one take. When Kazu makes a mistake she leaves it in and corrects it aloud, because that is how analysis really goes.

Tomás Ibarra mixes the sound, cuts the silences and writes the captions. Every caption is checked against the audio before a lesson goes online.

Lessons run 6 to 18 minutes. Short enough to finish, long enough to show one idea properly.

Captions are available in English, Chinese, Japanese, French and German.
